title: Automated detection labels with signal-detection outcomes and a label-accuracy manipulation
rationale: Automated Flagging raised accuracy by 4.4 points (95% CI [1.4, 7.3], p = 0.004; batches 3-4: 6.6), but accuracy alone cannot tell whether labels improve sensitivity or just push people to say 'AI'. Only 8 of 44 registered tests were significant, so a larger, focused sample with d-prime and criterion and a label-accuracy manipulation is needed.
contribution: Separates sensitivity from response bias for automated AI-detection labels and tests whether the benefit depends on label accuracy and persists without labels.
limitations: Posts and labels are simulated stimuli in a survey, not a real feed
Fixed label error rate tests only one level of inaccuracy

design.title: Automated detection labels: sensitivity vs bias
design.overview: Respondents are randomised to control, accurate automated labels, or labels wrong on a fixed share (25%) of posts. Each judges 24 posts (12 AI, 12 authentic) and then answers confidence and attitude items. A second wave days later shows fresh unlabeled posts to test carryover.
design.hypothesis: Accurate automated labels increase d-prime relative to control, with little change in criterion; inaccurate labels reduce d-prime and shift criterion.
design.primaryOutcome: d-prime computed from AI-post hits and authentic-post false alarms across 24 posts.
design.comparison: Accurate labels vs control, and inaccurate labels vs control and vs accurate labels, on d-prime, criterion, accuracy, AI-post detection and authentic-post detection; wave 2 compares the same measures without labels.
design.population: US adults from an online panel, about 400 per arm.

conditions.title: Automated Flagging accurate
conditions.description: Each post carries an automated AI-detection label that is correct for all posts.

conditions.title: Automated Flagging inaccurate
conditions.description: Each post carries an automated label that is wrong on a fixed 25% of posts.

questions.text: You are invited to a research study about how people judge online media. It takes about 10 minutes, is voluntary, and responses are anonymous. Do you consent to participate?
You will see 24 posts. For each, decide whether it is AI-generated. Go with your gut if unsure.
You will see 24 posts. For each, decide whether it is AI-generated. Each post carries a label from an automated AI-detection system, which will appear beside the post.
You will see 24 posts. For each, decide whether it is AI-generated. Each post carries a label from an automated AI-detection system, which will appear beside the post. The system is not perfect.
Is this post AI-generated? (Repeated for each of the 24 posts, shown in random order, 12 AI and 12 authentic.)
Please answer the following questions about artificial intelligence.

rows.text: I feel confident in my ability to detect artificial intelligence.
I think artificial intelligence technology is a threat to humans.

questions.text: Thank you. Some automated labels you saw may have been deliberately inaccurate to study how labels affect judgments. Please do not rely on them. You may be invited to a short follow-up in a few days.
Is this post AI-generated? (Repeated for 12 new unlabeled posts, 6 AI and 6 authentic.)

assumptions: Sample about 400 per arm (1,200 total): observed Automated Flagging effect 0.044 (batches 3-4: 0.066); H1 MDE 0.042 at n=127 vs 181, so 400 per arm detects about 0.028 at 80% power.
Posts 24 per respondent, half AI-generated, drawn from the source stimulus pool; the 25% label error rate is split evenly across AI and authentic posts.
Wave 2 fielded about 7 days later, with 12 fresh unlabeled posts; expect roughly 30% attrition.
d-prime uses log-linear correction for extreme rates.
unresolved: Actual image and video stimuli and label graphics must be supplied by the research team.
